notes.evidence: A service account represents an identity associated with an instance. Only one service account can be associated with an instance. You control access to the service account by controlling the grant of the Service Account User role for other IAM principals.

notes.front: How do priorities differ between firewall policy rules and VPC firewall rules?
notes.back: Policy rules: 0 to 2,147,483,547, no default, unique within the policy. VPC rules: 0 to 65,535, default 1000, may be shared.
notes.explanation: The comparison table sets range, default and uniqueness side by side.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC firewall rules”, “Priority”
notes.evidence: Range 0 to 2,147,483,547 0 to 65,535 Default priority number None 1000 (default) Uniqueness Must be unique within the policy Can be shared across rules

notes.front: In Shared VPC, how do host projects and service projects relate?
notes.back: A project cannot be both; there can be several host projects, but each service project attaches to only one host.
notes.explanation: So a service project cannot itself be a host project to further service projects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Shared VPC”, “Organizations, folders, and projects”
notes.evidence: A project cannot be both a host project and a service project simultaneously. Thus, a service project cannot be a host project to further service projects. You can create and use multiple host projects; however, each service project can only be attached to a single host project.

notes.front: How does Shared VPC differ from VPC Network Peering in scope?
notes.back: Shared VPC keeps one network in a host project for projects in the same organisation; peering connects separate networks, even across organisations.
notes.explanation: With Shared VPC, authorised principals in other projects use subnets of the one shared network.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC networks”, “Specifications”
notes.evidence: An organization can use Shared VPC to keep a VPC network in a common host project. Authorized IAM principals from other projects in the same organization can create resources that use subnets of the Shared VPC network. VPC networks can be connected to other VPC networks in different projects or organizations by using VPC Network Peering.

notes.front: Can one Cloud NAT gateway provide both Public NAT and Private NAT?
notes.back: No. A gateway provides one or the other; two separate gateways can serve the same subnet with both.
notes.explanation: Cloud NAT supports these two types of NAT.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud NAT overview”, “Types of Cloud NAT”
notes.evidence: Cloud NAT supports two types of NAT: Public NAT Private NAT A single Cloud NAT gateway provides either Public NAT or Private NAT. By creating two separate gateways, you can use both NAT types to serve the same subnet.

notes.front: When would you choose a proxy Network Load Balancer rather than a passthrough one?
notes.back: Proxy: a reverse proxy with advanced traffic controls and backends elsewhere. Passthrough: to keep client source addresses and use direct server return.
notes.explanation: Proxy load balancers support backends on-premises and in other clouds; passthrough ones return responses directly from backends.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Load Balancing overview”, “Network Load Balancers”
notes.evidence: Choose a proxy Network Load Balancer if you want to configure a reverse proxy load balancer with support for advanced traffic controls and backends on-premises and in other cloud environments. Choose a passthrough Network Load Balancer if you want to preserve the source IP address of the client packets, you prefer direct server return for responses,

notes.front: What is the difference between an external and an internal Google Cloud load balancer?
notes.back: External takes traffic from the internet into your VPC network; internal takes traffic from clients in or connected to that network.
notes.explanation: Internal clients can connect through VPC Network Peering or hybrid connections as well as from the same network.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a load balancer”, “External versus internal load balancing”
notes.evidence: External load balancers distribute traffic that comes from the internet to your Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. Internal load balancers distribute traffic that comes from clients in the same VPC network as the load balancer or clients connected to your VPC network by using VPC Network Peering, Cloud VPN, or Cloud Interconnect.

notes.front: What does Direct VPC egress trade for its lower latency and higher throughput, compared with a Serverless VPC Access connector?
notes.back: It uses more addresses in most cases; a connector uses fewer, but incurs extra VM charges.
notes.explanation: The comparison table lists latency, throughput, address use and cost for each method.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compare Direct VPC egress and VPC connectors”, “Comparison table”
notes.evidence: Latency Lower Higher Throughput Higher Lower IP allocation Uses more IP addresses in most cases Uses fewer IP addresses Cost No additional VM charges Incurs additional VM charges
